entities.summary:
Antiphanes, a prolific and innovative playwright who died around 333 BCE, stands as a pivotal figure in the development of Greek Middle Comedy, a genre bridging the political and fantastic satire of Old Comedy with the social realism of New Comedy. Active primarily in Athens during the mid-4th century BCE, his work significantly shaped the comedic landscape of the Classical Era. Alongside his contemporary Alexis, Antiphanes is regarded by scholars like Heinz-Günther Nesselrath as one of the most important writers of this transitional period, whose plays offered a diverse repertoire reflecting the evolving tastes and societal concerns of Athenian audiences.

Antiphanes' corpus was extraordinarily vast, with estimates ranging from 200 to 360 plays, though only fragments and titles survive today. His dramatic output explored a wide array of themes, frequently drawing upon mythological burlesque, where gods and heroes were depicted in human and often absurd situations, as seen in plays like "Antaios" or "Ganymedes." He also delved into social satire, portraying ordinary life, professions, and character types, foreshadowing the focus of New Comedy. His plays were characterized by intricate plots, witty dialogue, and a departure from the direct political commentary and chorus-centric structure of Old Comedy, favoring instead a more unified narrative and individual character development.
